key_insight: The paper highlights a growing, often unfounded surge of suspicion that academic manuscripts were produced by generative AI, and shows this trend is producing inconsistent, harmful responses across journals and reviewers.
problem_solved: Addresses the challenge of increasing accusations of AI-generated text in scholarly submissions—which can lead to false positives, reputational harm, uneven editorial practices, and a lack of clear, fair policies for investigation and disclosure.
method: Qualitative review of recent editorial decisions, public cases, and policy statements across journals to document trends and consequences.
Critical analysis of current AI-detection tools and their limitations, including risks of false positives and overreliance on automated methods.

Synthesis of ethical and procedural recommendations: a proposed framework for transparent, proportionate handling of suspected AI use (education, disclosure, careful verification, and safeguards for authors).
impact: This matters to AI/ML practitioners, editors, and institutions because it clarifies risks of knee-jerk policing, offers practicable safeguards to protect researcher reputation and scientific integrity, and guides fair policy-making around AI-assisted writing.
visual_elements: Timeline or heatmap showing the rise in reported AI-suspicion incidents and associated policy actions over recent years.
Flowchart for an editorial workflow when AI use is suspected (report → verify → consult author → remediate/resolve).
Illustrative chart comparing detector reliability (false positives/negatives) and annotations about contextual limitations.
Stakeholder diagram (authors, reviewers, editors, tool vendors, institutions) showing responsibilities and communication paths.
paper_title: On the troubling rise of generative AI suspicion in academic publishing
